accuracy.reason: Source-supported limits on freshness, retention, cache-aside ownership and outage fallback are accurate. Both diagrams match their card semantics; no automatic coherence or free-fallback guarantee is drawn.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.

mechanisms.reason: Eight card objectives have operational explanations: initial work, read paths, keys/ownership, stale-refill race, expiration/eviction, copy visibility, coalescing/admission limits and measured omission. The learner transfers these to new domains.

evidence.quote: The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: A product record stays the concrete example through read, write, removal, deployment and failure. Declared DB/instance/rate prerequisites suffice. Diagram arrows explicitly label stale-copy state rather than claiming propagation.

evidence.quote: In this example, the database owns the product record. Losing the cached copy must not lose the product.
Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold $20 while another holds $25.

decisions.reason: Benefits are balanced with memory and miss costs, strict checkout freshness, network/failure consequences and low-reuse omission. Failure response bounds source work rather than assuming available stale data.

evidence.quote: A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: Each unfamiliar cache concept is defined at its use, with concise examples. Coalescing explains sharing work, and the diagram makes both read paths explicit; there is enough detail for the stated reasoning questions.

evidence.quote: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.
Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.

outcomes.reason: C1: repeated expensive reads enable reuse. C2: station and language key transfers the taught currency-key mechanism. C3-4: hit/miss actor sequence and copy fill are correct. C5: application owns the read/fill, miss retains source cost and memory/lookup/write costs are named. Exact quotes substantiate the transfer.

C1-3: learner traces A capturing old hours, B committing/deleting, A refilling, then C returning old hours; slide 4 explicitly teaches that sequence and rejects unconditional freshness. C4: authoritative-source bypass is a justified transfer from checkout validation and the declared commit prerequisite.

C1-2: 12:03 stale hit, 12:11 expired miss and 12:05 evicted miss follow the taught entry lifetime/removal rules. C3-4: learner rejects guaranteed retention, source synchronization and automatic refresh, and distinguishes expiration from memory eviction; slide 5 plus miss flow support each.

C1-2: independent local copies survive another instance deletion; a single shared entry fits one-delete visibility under the question assumptions. C3-5: local in-process versus shared network access, operating cost and one-instance versus all-instance cache-access loss are explained without asserting total application failure or automatic DB coherence.

C1-2: simultaneous misses repeat source work; sharing an in-progress lookup reduces duplicates. C3-4: 10,000 fallback reads overwhelm 500/s capacity, so cap admitted source reads and reject excess. C5: primary response does not depend on a stale copy; optional stale use is explicitly conditional on accessibility and age and never assumes reading the failed cache. No advanced limiter implementation is required.

C1-2: rejects caching because each result has no subsequent reuse. C3: uses 2ms versus 100ms and 10/s versus 1000/s headroom. C4: added writes/storage/lookups are explicit. C5: repeated expensive or capacity-constrained reads prompt measurement rather than automatic caching. Slides 1/8 support all reasoning.

sourceChecks.claim: Microsoft caching guidance supports repeated-read reuse, latency/source-load benefit and copy overhead.
Microsoft cache-aside explicitly assigns cache check, source read, fill and return to the application.
Microsoft caching guidance supports keyed reusable copies and application management; distinct response inputs must not collide.
Microsoft cache-aside rejects unconditional consistency; given the stated asynchronous read/fill sequence, delete cannot cancel an older reader and refill can restore stale data.
Redis eviction documentation supports memory-driven LRU removal and noeviction rejection; expiration and eviction do not themselves perform source reads.
AWS caching guidance explains per-process independent caches, shared-cache network costs and common cache-outage dependency.
AWS describes thundering-herd source overload and request coalescing; finite dependency capacity requires restricting fallback rather than forwarding all requests.
Microsoft guidance conditions useful caching on reused and relatively expensive data; measurement and low-reuse omission follow directly.
